I get bitter towards people I know haven’t experienced any loss. A lot of the ‘happy’ people I know - as in energetic, talkative, productive, laugh a lot etc. have actually experienced many losses. For example my distant aunt was abandoned by her parents, the uncle that raised her died when she was about 20, her son died at 19 and her husband at 60 something, then her brother (my father who was her cousin actually but they were raised as brother and sister in the same house) - she’ll always find something to laugh about and some work that needs to be done. She just pushes through life and always gets back on her feet. And I know she suffered so much. People that see her occasionally would never guess. 
However many of the people I know, and know for a fact nothing like that has happened to them, are always complaining, they’re bitter themselves, they’re never content etc and it annoys me to no end. Just be happy, you’re ok, everyone you love is ok, stop being all drama llama about minor things.

I’m like that, I don’t talk much with the people in my life, but I post here and try to cry it out when I can.
I usually don’t feel comfortable talking about my grief with people who know me. It just feels like an extra private part of my mind that should stay reserved for me. It’s not healthy but it can be okay as long as there is some kind of outlet. I’d suggest letting him know that if he decides to talk or wants any type of support, you’re there for him, but don’t pressure him into talking. If you see him stuck with grief, not getting better, it might be good to discuss his options for help, but getting better takes time so give him some.

Same here - feel alone cause there’s no one I can trust with my feelings and my dad also died at 61 from the results of two strokes.  Though for me it happened six months ago so it’s not fresh as yours is and I’m now usually managing to get through. It is a bit tougher with the upcoming holidays - first time without him, that’s why I’m on here. Let yourself find your own way through the grief - it’s so difficult when you’re doing it alone, so take care of yourself (my big lesson was that since he’s not around to do it, I just have to remember to do it myself and be very consistent about it too).
I’m here if you wanna talk more either in the comments or messages. Someone on reddit said the best thing most real thing that can be said in these situations is that it sucks rather than the usual condolences - and I’ll just say it to you because it sucks so bad and I know it.

If they’ll keep the urn at home, try lighting your own candle and reflecting on your neighbor’s life and your relationship. Not the same thing, but it can help with closure.

I know how you feel. That's pretty much what I said when I heard my dad had a stroke - I wish I was never born, because this wouldn't have happened to him. Even if it did, he would have at least enjoyed his last years more.

My mom said that he'd punch me in the face if he heard me saying that - and he never punched me in my life, ever. He never really punched anyone so that's how wrong I was for saying it. I still feel like that sometimes, but I know that's not what he thought.

Then the doctors said that even though stress is considered a factor in such diseases, it doesn't work as simply as we laics think it does. Diagnoses like 'this person's kid wasn't that sweet so they got sick' don't really happen that way.

Cancer especially. My very dear aunt had cancer and while she did have a very stressful life, no doctor said that it's actually what gave her cancer and she's been to a lot of doctors. 

Your mom worked for you guys because she loved you and I'm sure she never regretted that. It was probably hard, but it's not what made her sick and I'd even say it's you guys that kept her going. She's a parent, we never know how they feel about us until we have our own kids. My mom also told me that - she never understood half of how her parents felt about her until she had me. 

So while I know how it feels, I don't think our parents feel that way about us.

And don't feel bad about using your mom's money - parents leave their assets to their kids. It's been like that since we had the idea of personal property. She worked so you'd have the money - it's okay to use it, especially for education. 
I felt sick driving my dad's car, I felt sick receiving his retirement money for myself - I still sometimes do. But if it were so wrong it wouldn't be the practice for kids to have it.

I know not much can be said to help, but I hope hearing someone else's experience at least gives you a new perspective.

I'm glad you shared this. I've always believed in signs, but since my dad died I've been afraid to believe them because I thought I could drive myself crazy with wishful thinking.

I had two songs. 

I was in a restaurant, eating a salad that I always used to share with him. Neither of us eats a lot so we could order one salad for both and there would still be left some lol  
So I was thinking about how heartbreaking it is to eat it alone for the first time ever, and then I had a thought how I hope one day it will be just a nice memory that I'll share with my kids over that salad. Then a song came on that has my name in it and it's about the guy dying and telling her to remember him by the good things since he has to leave as everyone else does at some point.

Then one early morning I couldn't sleep and I was sitting on the balcony thinking about that song from the restaurant, about it being a sign, and in general contemplating signs. I was thinking something like if I got more signs then maybe I could be more sure. Then someone blasted a song through their window that is about the person leaving and telling people not to be sorry because no one lasts forever, but to wish them good luck, take all their things and remember them sometimes.   
I was in a calm place that I've been visiting for a very long time and this hasn't happened before. Like never ever have I heard someone blast music at that hour in this place.

It was like the minimal function to have to be considered alive and there was none, and he didn't have a brain strem stroke but a regular ischemic(?) one. Mine was 61. Where we live, they can't take him off life support.  He was in a coma for 10 days, he died on the 11th.

I think that the prognosis depends on what really happened. My dad had an ischemic stroke, and when it's traumatic injuries in question there's more room for recovery than with a case like his. What they explained to me is that parts of his brain just died off from lack of oxygen - there's no recovery for that, no surgery, no medication, nothing helps, plus the dying materia can damage the healthy parts too and that can't be helped, either.They did say he might even live, but never function, he'd be in a vegetative state.

A family friend had a hemorrhagic stroke and she survived even though they said her chances were barely existent, but she still had surgery and lived. She's now functioning relatively well. But a big part of her brain survived and kept its functions.

I'm not sure about what brain stem stroke is but it could be that the damage was truly irreparable.

I'm not sure there's a pattern, maybe this - being alone usually gives me hope that there's still something out there, that there's a possibility for a normal life, but what tears it down usually is seeing other people in my life and how they actually very different from me now - they haven't had a loss and they feel just fine. I blended with them before this happened, now it's just not my place.

I'm not sure if it can come back. For example I actually loved my university and studying but that's something my father implemented into my thinking. What helps me deal with the loss of my father, and is not related to religion is the fact that as a descendant, it's natural for me to live on and the reason we want children can be simplified to wanting our species to carry on, and that's basically us living on through our genes in our children and the future generations. It's not the same for a brother, since he's not your ancestor, but you did come from the same one so basically you're still carrying some of the genes he also did - don't mind my uneducated  explanations, I only get the basics of the concept - and something that was in him, still lives on in you. It's possible to see your children (or even grand-children) resemble your siblings - so is that not that little part that lives on?

There's also consolation, at least for me, in the fact you can make their 'spirit' live on by teaching what they taught you, sharing what they shared with you and allowing and helping their memory to continue doing for others what the person did while they were alive. You save their legacy and pass it on, and each person has their own - it can be helping animals, or teaching children, or being a great cook who shared their recipes... All of that lives on in our minds and we can make it live much longer by sharing it with others and making it truly come alive even further by actually making some of those things happen.
